directAnswer: Blessed Gregory X was Tedaldo Visconti of Piacenza, an archdeacon on crusade in the Holy Land when he was elected on 1 September 1271 after a vacancy of nearly three years; he reigned until 10 January 1276. He convened the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, which proclaimed a short-lived reunion with the Greek Church and adopted his conclave law Ubi periculum.

sections.h2: Elected While on Crusade at Acre
paras: Tedaldo Visconti was born at Piacenza in northern Italy and made his career as a churchman rather than a scholar or bishop. He served as archdeacon of Liège and worked in the circle of influential prelates before joining the crusade led by the future King Edward I of England. He was in Acre in 1271 when news reached him that he had been chosen pope.

The election ended the longest vacancy in the Church's history. After Clement IV's death in 1268, the cardinals at Viterbo were deadlocked between French and Italian factions. Contemporary accounts report that the local authorities shut the electors in and restricted their food to force a decision. Finally a committee of six cardinals agreed on Tedaldo, who was not a cardinal and not yet a priest. He was ordained and consecrated in Rome in March 1272.

Gregory's heart remained with the Holy Land, and he called a general council to organize a new crusade, reform the Church and heal the schism with the East. The Second Council of Lyon opened in May 1274. Thomas Aquinas died on his way to it, and Bonaventure, one of its leading figures, died during the sessions.

Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII accepted a profession of faith that included the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and union with Rome was proclaimed. The agreement had little support among the Greek clergy and people and collapsed within a few years. The council also approved a crusade tithe, though no expedition ever sailed.

sections.h2: Ubi Periculum and the Rules of the Conclave
paras: Having seen the cost of a three-year vacancy, Gregory had the council adopt the constitution Ubi periculum. It required the cardinals to assemble in seclusion ten days after a pope's death, cut off from outside contact, with their food progressively reduced if they failed to elect. The word conclave, meaning a room locked with a key, comes from this arrangement.
Adrian V suspended the law in 1276, but Celestine V restored it and Boniface VIII placed it in canon law in 1298. Its core principles shaped papal elections into modern times.

Gregory also worked to restore order in the Empire, which had lacked a generally recognized ruler for years. He supported the election of Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans in 1273, persuaded the rival claimant Alfonso of Castile to give up his claim, and met Rudolf at Lausanne in 1275.

Returning toward Rome, Gregory fell ill and died at Arezzo on 10 January 1276. He was buried in Arezzo's cathedral, where he was venerated locally. Pope Clement XI confirmed his cult in 1713, and the Church honors him as Blessed.

keyFacts: Born Tedaldo Visconti at Piacenza; elected while at Acre in 1271
Election ended a vacancy of almost three years (1268–1271)
Convened the Second Council of Lyon (1274), which proclaimed union with the Greeks
Issued Ubi periculum, the law that created the conclave system
Supported Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans
Died at Arezzo, 10 January 1276; cult confirmed by Clement XI in 1713

faqs.question: Why is Gregory X important for papal elections?
faqs.answer: His constitution Ubi periculum, adopted at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, required cardinals to be locked in seclusion until they elected a pope. It is the origin of the conclave.

faqs.question: Did the Second Council of Lyon end the East-West schism?
faqs.answer: It proclaimed a reunion after Byzantine envoys accepted a Catholic profession of faith, but the union was rejected by most of the Greek Church and did not last.

faqs.question: Is Gregory X a saint?
faqs.answer: He is a Blessed. His long-standing local veneration at Arezzo was confirmed by Pope Clement XI in 1713.
